claim.pdf_says: Items 'c)', 'd)' and 'e)' are indented one level, subordinate to item '2) When the value of operand-2 is greater than zero, the results shall be determined as follows:' (begun on page 208); items '3)' and '4)' then return to the outer margin.
claim.markdown_says: c) When operand-2 is an integer and the following condition is true ... e) Otherwise, the equivalent arithmetic expression is defined by the implementor. ... 3) When operand-2 is less than zero, ... 4) When both operand-1 and operand-2 are equal to zero, ...   (c/d/e written flush left, at the same indentation as 3) and 4))
claim.why_it_matters: In 8.8.1.4.4 the a)-e) cases apply only when operand-2 is greater than zero, whereas 3) and 4) are independent rules. Page 208 does indent a) and b) three spaces under 2); losing the indentation for c)-e) at the page break detaches them from their parent and makes them look like peers of 3) and 4).

verdict.reasoning:
CONFIRMED by independent pixel measurement of the 300-dpi render plus a read of the markdown source; I tried to refute it on all four standard grounds and each attempt failed.

(1) Is the indentation actually there in the PDF? Yes, and it is not a judgement call. I measured the leftmost dark pixel of every text-line band in E:/Temp/specrecon/v209/spec_p209.png (2550x3300 @ 300dpi). List-marker x-origins: 'c)' y=494 left=409; 'd)' y=915 left=409; 'e)' y=1337 left=409; '3)' y=1600 left=337; '4)' y=1864 left=335. The hanging-indent continuation lines corroborate the same one-level step: e)'s runover lines (y=1390/1442/1495) sit at left=482 while 3)'s runover 'expression' (y=1663) sits at left=409. So marker-to-marker and runover-to-runover the offset is a consistent ~73 px = 0.24 in at 300 dpi, i.e. exactly one nesting level. For the outer margin: the 8.8.1.5 heading (y=2021) and all body paragraphs (y=2232-2905) sit at left=334-336, the same column as '3)' and '4)'. c)/d)/e) are demonstrably NOT at the outer margin.

(2) Is the markdown really flat? Yes. specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 9083, 9091, 9099 ('c)', 'd)', 'e)') and lines 9101, 9105 ('3)', '4)') all begin at column 0 with zero leading whitespace. The intra-item display lines under c) and d) -- '(operand-2 = 3)' (9085), 'the equivalent expression shall be' (9087), '((operand-1 * operand-1) * operand-1)' (9089), and the d) analogues at 9093/9095/9097 -- are likewise flush left at column 0.

(3) Could this be a global transcription convention that flattens all lists, making the page-209 rendering merely stylistic rather than a defect? This is the strongest refutation available and it fails on the evidence. The SAME transcription preserves the identical nesting one page earlier: line 9062 puts '2) When the value of operand-2 is greater than zero, the results shall be determined as follows:' at column 0; lines 9064 and 9072 indent 'a)' and 'b)' by exactly 3 spaces under it; and lines 9066/9068/9070/9074 indent a)'s and b)'s display lines by 6 spaces. Page 208 also indents 'NOTE 4' (line 9042) by 3 spaces under item 1) and the '(1)' display line (9060) by 3. So the convention is established, applied, and then dropped precisely at the page-209 boundary. The transcription is internally inconsistent with itself across a page break, which is the definition of a page-break transcription defect rather than a house style.

(4) Does it change meaning? Yes, which is why 'cosmetic' understates it. Read as transcribed, the enumeration on page 209 presents c), d), e), 3), 4) as five peers of one list. Item e) reads 'Otherwise, the equivalent arithmetic expression is defined by the implementor' -- as a flush-left peer its 'Otherwise' scopes against 3) and 4), i.e. against the operand-2 < 0 and the 0**0 cases, rather than against a) through d) inside the operand-2 > 0 branch. The guard 'When the value of operand-2 is greater than zero' is silently stripped from c), d) and e). A reader or downstream extractor working from the markdown alone would conclude that the implementor-defined fallback applies to negative exponents too, when in the actual standard 3) mandates a specific expression (1 / (operand-1 ** FUNCTION ABS (operand-2))) for that case. That is a substantive misreading of 8.8.1.4.4, not a whitespace nit.

(5) Misquote check: none. The claim's PDF description matches the render, its markdown excerpt matches lines 9083/9099/9101/9105 verbatim, and its statement that page 208 indents a) and b) by three spaces is exactly what line 9064/9072 do. Every particular of the claim checks out.

Refutation attempts exhausted; the finding stands.
verdict.corrected_description:
The claim is accurate as written and needs no correction of fact; two refinements are worth recording.

SCOPE IS WIDER THAN THE THREE MARKERS. The flattening is not limited to the 'c)', 'd)', 'e)' labels -- every subordinate display line inside c) and d) is flattened to column 0 as well: '(operand-2 = 3)', 'the equivalent expression shall be', '((operand-1 * operand-1) * operand-1)', '(operand-2 = 4)', 'the equivalent expression shall be', '((operand-1 * operand-1) * (operand-1 * operand-1))' (ISO_COBOL.md lines 9085-9097). In the PDF these sit at left=629 and left=554 versus the c)/d) marker at left=409, i.e. one and two further levels in; page 208 correctly renders the a)/b) equivalents at 6 spaces. The fix is to indent lines 9083-9099 by 3 spaces (markers) and 6 spaces (display/body sub-lines) to match the established page-208 convention, restoring the a)-e) run to a single consistent level.

SEVERITY SHOULD BE RAISED FROM COSMETIC TO STRUCTURAL/SEMANTIC. Losing the level does not merely look wrong; it reparents c)-e) out of the 'operand-2 greater than zero' branch of 8.8.1.4.4 and makes e)'s 'Otherwise' fallback appear to govern the negative-exponent and 0**0 cases that 3) and 4) define explicitly. Any rule extraction driven off the markdown would mis-derive exponentiation semantics.

RELATED BUT SEPARATE, NOT A CONTENT LOSS: the PDF's first physical line on page 209 is the display expression '(operand-1 * operand-1)' (y=388, left=629), the equivalent expression for item b). The markdown does not carry it on page 209; it was merged onto the tail of page 208 line 9076 as 'the equivalent expression shall be (operand-1 * operand-1)'. The text therefore survives and no content is lost -- only the display-line break and the page assignment differ -- so this does not constitute a separate discrepancy, but it is the same page-break handling weakness that produced the indentation loss and should be fixed alongside it.
